sections.b: Daniel 1 to 3 tell of a Jewish exile and his three friends taken to Babylon: the food test, Nebuchadnezzar's dream of the statue, and the golden statue and the furnace. All three are set in Nebuchadnezzar's reign. They belong to the Daniel "court tale" type (Joseph, Esther) and carry the book's themes: God gives and takes kingdoms, and faithful people can serve a foreign king and keep God's law. Chapter 2 changes from Hebrew to Aramaic at verse 4 and the Aramaic continues to 7:28.

sections.h: Two layers of date and two audiences
sections.b: Readers date the book to the sixth century BC (Daniel in Babylon and Persia) or to 167-164 BC, when Antiochus IV persecuted the Jews. The first dating reads the stories and visions as true prophecy to the exiles. The second reads the stories as older tales gathered and the visions as written for the persecuted. A third view takes the tales as earlier and the visions as Maccabean. The opening pages of the book state the evidence for each.

common: Daniel was written in Babylon and Persia by the Daniel of the stories (traditional view).
Many scholars date the whole book to 167-164 BC, with the court tales older.
uncommon: The Aramaic chapters (2-7) and the Hebrew chapters are two collections joined by an editor.

sections.h: Babylon in the Daniel court tales
sections.b: In Daniel 1 to 3 Babylon is the capital of a vast empire with a trained class of scholars, the Chaldeans, who read omens and advise the king. Daniel and his friends are trained in its schools, given Babylonian names and put to work in its administration. Shinar, the old name for Babylonia, links the setting to the tower of Babel, and the golden statue stands on a plain in the province of Babylon. The tales present the city as grand and godless, but not as a place God has left.

The king appears as the conqueror who takes the temple vessels (1:1-2), the dreamer who can find no one to tell his dream (2), the man who falls on his face before Daniel (2:46) and the builder of the golden statue (3). He confesses the God of Daniel twice (2:47; 3:28) and does not give up his own gods. Daniel calls him the head of gold, a king given his kingdom by God (2:37-38); Jeremiah calls him God's servant (Jeremiah 27:6). The historical Nebuchadnezzar II (605-562 BC) is known from the Babylonian Chronicles and his building inscriptions, which do not mention these events.

sections.b: Daniel 1 to 3 give a picture of Jewish life in exile that differs from Lamentations and Psalm 137: people are trained at court, rise to office, and meet tests of loyalty. The test of the king's food, the refusal to worship the statue and the furnace show the limits of what a Jew in exile will give the state. Jeremiah's letter had told the exiles to seek the city's good (Jeremiah 29:7); Daniel shows how far that goes.

sections.h: Daniel and his friends as court officials
sections.b: Ashpenaz is called the chief of the court officials (sarisim), the word the site renders "eunuchs", and the young men he trains might become the same kind of official. Isaiah's word that Hezekiah's sons would serve as eunuchs in Babylon (Isaiah 39:7) was read by some of the rabbis as fulfilled in Daniel and his friends, and the Talmud records that Rav took it literally and Rabbi Hanina figuratively (Sanhedrin 93b). The Hebrew text of Daniel does not say they were made eunuchs.

uncommon: Daniel and his friends were physically made eunuchs (Rav in the Talmud).

sections.h: Daniel's refusal of the king's food
sections.b: Daniel 1:8 says he "defiled himself" with the king's food and wine, without naming the law behind it. Four explanations are given: forbidden meat, food offered to idols, the obligation of eating at the king's table, and general piety. Judith (Judith 12:2) and Tobit (Tobit 1:10-11) show a later Jewish custom of refusing Gentile food, and 2 Maccabees 5:27 and 6:18-20 show the same under persecution.

common: Daniel refused the food because it was unclean meat.
uncommon: The food test shows that a plant diet is healthier than meat.

sections.b: Nebuchadnezzar's dream is a royal dream of the kind the ancient Near East expected the learned men to interpret by manuals. The Babylonian experts fail, and Daniel succeeds because God shows him the secret. As Joseph before Pharaoh, he says that interpretation comes from God (Genesis 40:8; Genesis 41:16; Daniel 2:28, 30). Daniel's own gift for visions and dreams is set out in 1:17.

The book of Daniel is written partly in Aramaic: Daniel 2:4b to 7:28, with Hebrew before and after. The text itself marks the point with the word aramit "in Aramaic". The reasons for the change are debated (the Chaldeans' own speech, a collection of Aramaic stories, the chiastic design of chapters 2 to 7, a readership in the diaspora). The Aramaic of Daniel has Persian and a few Greek loanwords, and the dating of its dialect is part of the argument over the book's date.

sections.h: The golden statue as state worship
sections.b: In Daniel 3 the king calls officials from the whole empire to bow to a golden statue when the music sounds; the penalty for refusal is death by fire. No Babylonian text records such a demand, and the story is read by some as a tale shaped by later experience: Antiochus IV's decree that his whole kingdom be one people (1 Maccabees 1:41-43) and the Roman demand for sacrifice to the emperor. Revelation 13:14-15 draws on the same scene. Whatever its date, the chapter became a standard text for refusing state worship.

The golden statue (Aramaic tselem, the word for "image" in Genesis 1:26) is the Bible's picture of an idol the state makes. The prophets mocked such objects (Isaiah 44:9-20) and Daniel 3 turns the mockery into narrative: the statue is worshiped by the whole empire and is powerless to save the empire's own soldiers from the furnace. Churches that forbid images and those that venerate them each cite the scene in their own way.

Daniel 2 gives a statue of gold, silver, bronze, iron and clay that is broken by a stone (2:31-35); Daniel 3 gives a golden statue that peoples worship (3:1-7). The first image is a picture of kingdoms and the second is an actual idol, but the writer plays on the same word, tselem. The three friends' refusal (3:18) is the biblical story most often told about refusing idolatry under threat.

sections.h: The three in the furnace as martyr models
sections.b: The speech "and if he does not" (Daniel 3:18) made Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego examples of faithful refusal. 1 Maccabees 2:59-60 names them with Daniel among those who were saved by faith; 4 Maccabees 16:21 includes them in its list of examples for a mother and her seven sons; First Clement 45:6-7 puts them among the persecuted righteous. The Talmud (Pesachim 53b) treats them as examples of giving one's life to sanctify God's name. They are also in Hebrews 11:34, where "put out the power of fire" probably alludes to them.

sections.h: The stone that becomes a mountain
sections.b: Daniel 2:44 is among the clearest Old Testament statements of a kingdom of God that replaces human empires: a kingdom the God of the heavens will raise, not left to another people, that will end all the others and stand forever. Chapter 7 will give it to "the people of the holy ones of the Most High" (7:27). Readers differ on when it comes (in the Maccabean crisis, in Christ, at the end), and whether the stone is a person, a people or a reign.

The phrase "in the last days" opens Daniel's explanation of the dream. In Aramaic it matches the Hebrew idiom that in the prophets can mean a later time or the end. Revelation takes the phrase from Theodotion's Greek for its own opening ("what must soon take place", Revelation 1:1), which shows how the early church read Daniel 2.

sections.h: Daniel's place and the Greek additions
sections.b: The Hebrew Bible puts Daniel among the Writings (the Talmud lists it between Lamentations and Esther, Bava Batra 14b); Christian Bibles put it among the Prophets after Ezekiel. The Greek Daniel is longer than the Hebrew and Aramaic: the Prayer of Azariah and the Song of the Three (inside chapter 3), Susanna and Bel and the Dragon. Catholic and Orthodox churches count these as Scripture; Protestants set them among the Apocrypha. The book's "Where Christians differ" card gives each church's own statement.

The Greek Daniel contains three additions that are not in the Hebrew and Aramaic text: the Prayer of Azariah and the Song of the Three, inserted at Daniel 3:23-24; Susanna; and Bel and the Dragon. They are works.json Additions to Daniel, deuterocanonical for Catholic and Orthodox churches. This edition's Plain English Translation translates only the Hebrew and Aramaic and treats the additions as variants, as for Esther.

The king says God "sent his angel" (3:28), the first angel in the book (the "watchers" of 4:13 are holy ones from heaven but are not called angels). The Greek Prayer of Azariah has the angel of the Lord come down into the furnace and drive out the flame (Theodotion 3:49). The angel who guards the faithful also shuts the lions' mouths (6:22).

sections.h: 'A son of the gods' in Daniel 3:25
sections.b: Nebuchadnezzar's phrase bar-'elahin is not the Christian title: it is a pagan king's way of saying a divine being. The KJV's "the Son of God" reads Christian language into his mouth. Theodotion's Greek, "like a son of God", and the Old Greek, "like an angel of God", already differ, and the Church Fathers and later Jewish writers each read the figure their own way (see the note).

common: The fourth man in the furnace was Jesus.
uncommon: The fourth man was an angel (the king's own word for him in 3:28; Jewish and some Christian readers).

sections.b: Daniel 1:1 puts the first siege in Jehoiakim's third year, while Jeremiah 25:1 and 46:2 say fourth for the same event (605 BC). The explanations are different counting of the first year, two Babylonian campaigns (605 and 604), or a schematic date. Daniel 2:1 says the second year of Nebuchadnezzar, after three years of training (1:5), another difficulty. The Greek date for the statue is the eighteenth year (3:1), the year before Jerusalem fell. The site dates the fall of Jerusalem to 586 BC.

sections.b: Daniel 1:21 ends the chapter in the first year of Cyrus, as a note that Daniel outlived Babylon. The book later gives Cyrus the third year of a vision (10:1) and has a Darius the Mede take the kingdom first (5:31). Cyrus' own record is the Cylinder (539 BC), which presents him as restoring the gods of Babylon and returning peoples.

Nebuchadnezzar sees a statue with a head of gold, chest and arms of silver, belly and thighs of bronze, legs of iron, and feet part iron and part clay; a stone cut "not by hands" strikes the feet, the whole statue is crushed and the stone becomes a mountain. Daniel names the head as Nebuchadnezzar (2:38); the rest of the sequence is not named. The stone is a kingdom the God of the heavens will set up (2:44).

The readings of the Jewish medieval commentators (for example Rashi) and of the later churches are given at Daniel 7 and Daniel 8, where the beasts and the ram and goat name more of the kingdoms.

sections.h: The three friends in Daniel 1 to 3
sections.b: Hananiah, Mishael and Azariah, renamed Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego, share Daniel's training and his refusal of the king's food (1:6-7), pray with him (2:17-18), are given charge of the province of Babylon at his request (2:49), and are the only ones to defy the golden statue (3:12). They are thrown into the furnace and rescued by God's angel (3:28). They are not named in the later chapters of the book.
